title: Filtering Collections
learning_outcomes: Explain how filtering collections affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from equality filters to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on filtering collections in filtering, sorting, searching, and pagination. You will connect equality filters to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Filtering Collections matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying equality filters deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Collection endpoints need explicit parameter validation, stable ordering, bounded result sizes, and predictable pagination metadata. In this lesson, treat “Filtering Collections” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating filtering collections as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
